issues.legal_issue: Exempting public housing property from rent-control protections does not deny equal protection merely because tenants of cooperative housing societies remain protected when the societies and their tenants are not shown to be similarly situated.
material_facts: The challenged amendment excluded land and buildings belonging to or vested in the housing board from rent-control protections.
The board was established to frame housing schemes and address an acute shortage of accommodation, was controlled by the government, and had no shareholders interested in distributing profits.

Cooperative housing societies could earn profits distributable to their members, and no evidence established that they had tenants in a relationship comparable to the occupants of the board's properties.
issues.conclusion: The comparison with cooperative housing societies did not establish discrimination, and the amendment was not unconstitutional on this ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under article 14 of the Constitution, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia that distinguishes the grouped persons or things from others and must bear a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court relied on article 14 and section 3-A of the Bombay Housing Board Act, inserted by the 1951 amendment; it relied on no earlier cases.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_rent_exemption and public_housing_body and board_has_no_profit_motive and cooperative_societies_may_distribute_profits and no_evidence_of_comparable_tenancy

predicates.equality_challenge_to_rent_exemption: A litigant challenged an exemption from rent-control protections as unequal treatment under a constitutional equality guarantee.
predicates.public_housing_body: A public body was created to address housing needs through housing schemes.
predicates.board_has_no_profit_motive: The public housing body was government-controlled and had no shareholders interested in distributing profits.
predicates.cooperative_societies_may_distribute_pro: The compared cooperative societies could earn profits distributable to their members.
predicates.no_evidence_of_comparable_tenancy: The litigant produced no evidence that the compared societies had tenants in a relationship comparable to the occupants of the public body's property.

issues.definition: When an equality challenge concerns a rent-protection exemption for a public housing body, and the body lacks a profit motive while the proposed cooperative comparison may involve distributable profits and lacks evidence of comparable tenancies, the comparison does not establish a denial of equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: Exempting tenants of government or public-authority housing from rent-control protections while protecting tenants of private landlords does not deny equal protection when the classes are differently situated and the distinction serves the public housing purpose.
material_facts: The rent-control law exempted premises belonging to the government or a local authority, and the amendment expressly extended an exemption to land and buildings belonging to or vested in the housing board.
The board was established to address an acute shortage of accommodation and was controlled by the government.

The Court considered that government and public housing bodies would not be expected to act from a profit-making motive to raise rents unduly or eject tenants, unlike private landlords who might do so.
issues.conclusion: The difference in treatment rested on an intelligible distinction rationally related to the public purpose of addressing the need for housing; neither section 4 nor section 3-A violated article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification based on an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court held that tenants of government, local-authority, or housing-board property were not on an equal footing with tenants of private landlords because public bodies served a housing purpose and were not expected to act for profit. The Court relied on article 14, section 4 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and section 3-A of the Bombay Housing Board Act; it relied on no earlier cases.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_rent_exemption and public_housing_body and public_body_has_housing_mandate and public_body_not_expected_to_seek_profit and private_landlords_may_seek_profit

predicates.equality_challenge_to_rent_exemption: A litigant challenged an exemption from rent-control protections as unequal treatment under a constitutional equality guarantee.
predicates.public_housing_body: A public body owned or managed housing property.
predicates.public_body_has_housing_mandate: The public body was established to address housing needs and accommodation shortages.
predicates.public_body_not_expected_to_seek_profit: The public body was not expected to act from a profit-making motive to raise rents unduly or eject occupants.
predicates.private_landlords_may_seek_profit: Private landlords could act from a profit-making motive in setting rents or seeking to remove tenants.

issues.definition: When an equality challenge concerns different rent protections for public and private housing, a public housing mandate and the different profit incentives attributed to public bodies and private landlords mean the distinction does not deny equal protection.
